https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/labo.title: Labour pledges ban on perks as water bosses take £26m in bonuses
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/labo.subtitle: Tories accused of  ‘turning a blind eye to corruption at heart of the industry’ as firms face showdown over sewage spills
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/labo.text:
Labour has promised to ban bonuses for polluting water companies after finding chief executives received £26 million in bonuses and long-term incentives since the last election.
The party said it would give regulators the power to end the use of bonuses if companies cause illegal discharges.
The heads of the privatised water firms will also meet Steve Barclay, the environment secretary, on Tuesday, The Times can reveal, to discuss their progress on curbing spills from storm overflows.
Barclay has been told by Rishi Sunak that he must hold water companies to account, after his predecessor Thérèse Coffey, faced criticism for not doing enough to improve rivers. Only 14 per cent of England’s rivers are classified as “good”, or close to their natural state.
On the agenda will be whether water firms are doing enough maintenance on sewer networks.
Barclay has told company leaders that he thinks 20 per cent of sewage spills are happening because of a lack of maintenance, including clearing fatbergs and other blockages. He has said that these spills must stop by the end of the year.
Privately, however, figures in the water industry dispute the figure and claim it is closer to 2 per cent. In the wake of The Times’ Clean it Up campaign, companies have promised to spend £10 billion reducing sewage spills by 2030, provided they get a provisional green light from economic regulator Ofwat this summer.
Six of the nine main wastewater firms in England were criticised recently for failing to deliver real-time sewage spill maps by the end of last year as pledged.
Multiple sources in the industry said the reason for the delay was that executives did not want to anger Barclay by releasing maps that sparked a flurry of headlines about raw sewage discharges, as happened when Thames Water published its dashboard a year ago. A government source said they did not recognise that reason, and noted the legal deadline is 2025.
While most sewage spills are considered legal under permits issued by the Environment Agency, there are growing concerns among watchdogs and campaigners of illegal spilling. One release of raw sewage that had been under way for three months — bar a one-hour hiatus on December 3 — finally ceased on January 19 at a Southern Water storm overflow near Bognor Regis.
“In the three years that we have been campaigning, we’ve never seen a pollution incident come close to this before,” said Ed Acteson, of campaign group Whitstable SOS. “Water companies are only supposed to release sewage when certain thresholds are met and the rainfall is so heavy that the pumping stations are in danger of becoming overwhelmed. There is simply no way that those conditions were met for three consecutive months.”
Another company, United Utilities, was recently accused of downgrading the severity of sewage pollution cases across northwest England, including one at Windermere.
Environment Agency insiders told Panorama that the firm had wrongly reclassified scores of incidents last year. The firm rejected the charge but it was seized on by Labour, which the party said showed “corruption at the heart of the water industry.”
Labour cited that case today as a reason it would plough ahead with giving Ofwat powers to ban bonuses for firms that spilled sewage illegally, reiterating a pledge from its party conference. In a new analysis, the opposition found that firms had paid out £10.7 billion to chief executives since 2019.
The data shows that around £3 million was paid out in each of the initial years, but the amount roughly halved last year as several bosses including the heads of Southern Water and Thames Water waived their bonus amid anger over spills.
“This Conservative government has wilfully turned a blind eye to corruption at the heart of the water industry,” said Steve Reed, the shadow environment secretary. “The result is stinking, toxic sewage destroying our countryside, and consumers facing higher bills while failing water bosses pocket millions in bonuses,” he added.
A government spokesman said: “Our Plan for Water is delivering more investment, stronger regulation, and tougher enforcement — and we have already been very clear that water companies must never profit from environmental damage.”
A Water UK spokesperson said: “We agree that any financial reward should be tightly linked to performance – including protecting the environment. It is also right that regulators have all the powers they feel they need to hold water companies to account.”
